newsitem.title: USA: Wilmington operating but beach communities hard hit.
newsitem.headline: Wilmington operating but beach communities hard hit.

text.p: The city of Wilmington resumed a semblance of normal life on Friday as residents cleaned up streets and some shops opened, but its battered beach communities were under 24-hour curfew and likely to be closed for days.

Hurricane Fran's 100 mph winds and its eye passed directly over the city, which is no stranger to hurricanes. Residents of surrounding New Hanover County were under a 10 p.m.-to-6 a.m. curfew until further notice.

While much of Wilmington, a city of 60,000 on the Cape Fear River, remained without electricity Friday, a few gas stations, shops and restaurants opened their doors and did a brisk business in ice, drinks, gasoline and snack food.
But Wilmington's seaside towns of Wrightsville Beach, Carolina Beach and Kure Beach were closed to all but officials, power crews, engineers -- and heavy equipment.
"This was a very devastating storm," said Betty Medlin, mayor of Kure Beach, who said at the height of the storm waves were 15-25 feet above normal at the beach in her town.
"We have a lot of structural damage, streets washed out. We have water and sewer lines that were ruptured and it's going to take some time to get them back together."

Journalists and television crews, along with residents, were kept from the islands about 15 miles south of Wilmington, but officials who had surveyed the damage described streets covered with sand from Fran's powerful tidal surge, which undermined some beachfront buildings and sent them tumbling into the surf.
"Much of downtown Carolina Beach is under water," said town councilman Rick Burroughs.
National Guards and police from South Carolina patroled the streets to deter looting while wildlife and marine patrol officers watched waterways between the islands and the mainland.

Wrightsville Beach city manager Tony Caudle estimated it could be four to seven days before residents were allowed to return, citing the complete absence of electricity, water and sewer service to the islands.

"There's a real concern about safety here," he said. "If we let residents back, when dark comes, the first thing they're going to do is pull out a candle or a kerosene lamp. If there's a fire, we would have no hope of fighting that fire."
Wilmington Mayor Don Betz said a preliminary damage assessment in his city indicated one percent of buildings were destroyed, 24 percent sustained major damage and 75 percent minor damage.

Water and sewer services were operating, but the city remained only partially functional with trees blocking streets and only a handful of traffic lights operating. Officials implemented a ban on burning storm debris to limit the chance of fire.
